result.question:
Patenting a registration-free intraoperative vertebral level identification method: what a US-based academic physician-inventor must do, in what order, and by when.

The technique: naming vertebrae on limited-field intraoperative radiographs and fluoroscopy WITHOUT registering to a preoperative CT or MRI, by (a) linking a short series of overlapping C-arm exposures into a patient-specific chain that substitutes for registration, (b) a sequence model over per-vertebra embeddings trained on mixed band lengths, (c) a selective-prediction/conformal output that abstains or returns a region rather than a single name, and (d) explicit handling of transitional anatomy (lumbosacral and thoracolumbar variants) including a disc-based delimitation rule.

ALREADY ESTABLISHED, do not re-derive - build on it: US 11,284,846 (Siemens Healthineers + Johns Hopkins, priority 2011-05-12, expiry 2034-09-14) has ONE independent claim whose step (a) requires "acquiring a preoperative 3D computer-tomography (CT) image of a vertebra". US 10,368,956 (Johns Hopkins, priority 2016-02-16, expiry 2037-02-16) has four independent claims, each requiring "a preoperative 3D magnetic resonance image of a subject". Both therefore appear not to read on a CT-free method under the all-elements rule.

1. PRIOR ART AND FREEDOM TO OPERATE. The full INPADOC/simple families and US continuations/divisionals of both patents above - do any family member claim vertebra labelling WITHOUT a preoperative 3D volume? Also any other granted or pending claims, from any assignee, on: vertebra labelling from radiographs alone; image stitching or long-length/slot-scan imaging of the spine; C-arm panoramas; sequence models over vertebra embeddings; abstention/conformal prediction in medical imaging. Distinguish blocking claims from prior-art-only disclosures.
2. ELIGIBILITY. Software/AI medical-imaging claims under 35 USC 101 after Alice: which claim forms survive at the USPTO and Federal Circuit, the 2019 and later PTO subject-matter eligibility guidance applied to diagnostic imaging algorithms, and how successful applicants tie claims to a concrete imaging apparatus or an acquisition protocol rather than to a mathematical result.
3. DISCLOSURE CLOCK. The 35 USC 102(b) one-year US grace period versus absolute novelty in EP/JP/CN: what counts as an enabling public disclosure - journal article, preprint, conference abstract or poster, public code repository, publicly reachable web demo, released model weights. Whether a private-by-link or access-controlled deployment counts. What a provisional filed before publication preserves, and what is lost the day the paper goes out.
4. UNIVERSITY OWNERSHIP. How US university IP policies assign inventions by faculty and by resident/clinical staff, what an invention disclosure to a tech transfer office triggers, timelines, revenue sharing, what happens if the university declines to file, and how inventor-retained rights are handled. Wayne State University's stated policy specifically if public.
5. MECHANICS AND COST. Provisional -> non-provisional -> PCT national phase: real deadlines, realistic attorney and filing costs at each stage, micro/small entity status, Track One prioritised examination, and what a provisional must actually contain (enablement and written description) to support later claims rather than failing as a placeholder.
6. WHAT NOT TO PATENT. Where trade secret beats a patent for trained weights and training-data curation, given that a patent publishes the method.

For every claim: cite the statute, case, patent number or policy document. Distinguish black-letter rules from practitioner convention. Flag anything jurisdiction-dependent or recently changed.

confirmed.claim: The patent issued with only three claims total (claim 1 independent, claims 2 and 3 dependent), so there is no alternative independent claim that omits the preoperative-CT step; the C-arm limitation appears only in dependent claim 3, which narrows rather than broadens scope and still inherits step (a)'s preoperative CT requirement.

confirmed.claim: Registration of the preoperative 3D volume onto the 2D intraoperative image is itself a required claim element (the final display step of claims 1 and 11), so a registration-free pipeline omits a second independent limitation beyond the 3D-volume acquisition step.
confirmed.quote: providing, by the device and for display, a visual representation of the 3D magnetic resonance image data registered onto the 2D image data of the subject.

confirmed.claim: The specification discloses automatic vertebra labeling on intraoperative x-ray/fluoroscopy for wrong-level prevention, but only in the registration-dependent form (labels defined in the 3D image overlaid on the 2D image), making this patent prior-art disclosure against a registration-free labeling method's novelty/obviousness rather than a blocking claim.
confirmed.quote: The approach is analogous to a previous method (the 'LevelCheck' algorithm) in which a preoperative 3D image (viz., CT) is registered to a 2D projection image, and labels defined in the 3D image can thereby be overlaid on the 2D image (e.g., labels of spinal vertebrae).

confirmed.claim: Unlike US 11,284,846 and US 10,368,956, no independent claim of US 8,718,346 B2 requires a preoperative 3D CT or MRI volume — all four independent claims (1, 33, 36, 47) require only 'a high resolution baseline image of the surgical field', and dependent claim 2 makes CT merely one option alongside a pre-procedure fluoroscopic image. The 'no preoperative 3D volume' argument that clears the Siemens/JHU patents therefore does NOT clear this patent, and a separate non-infringement theory is required.
confirmed.quote: 1. A method for generating a display of an image of a patient's internal anatomy in a surgical field during a medical procedure, comprising: acquiring a high resolution baseline image of the surgical field including the patient's internal anatomy in a baseline orientation; ... 2. The method of claim 1, wherein the baseline image is one of a pre-procedure full dose fluoroscopic image or a CT scan image. 3. The method of claim 1, wherein the baseline image is a DRR.

confirmed.claim: US 8,718,346 discloses, but does not claim, stitching multiple C-arm fluoroscopic exposures taken at different locations into a composite base image / composite field of view. This is prior-art-only against element (a) of the proposed invention (linking overlapping C-arm exposures into a patient-specific chain): it is a printed publication with a 2011-10-05 priority and a 2014-05-06 grant date, so it is 35 USC 102(a)(1) art that will be cited against any claim reciting C-arm image stitching or panorama formation per se, but it creates no blocking claim on stitching.
confirmed.quote: In some cases where the C-arm is moved during the procedure, multiple high resolution images can be obtained at different locations in the surgical site, and then these multiple images stitched together to form a composite base image (as discussed below). ... whether a current movement of the C-arm would result in an image that cannot be correlated or registered with any baseline image, or that cannot be stitched together with other images to form a composite field of view.

confirmed.claim: US 8,718,346 discloses placing vertebral level labels ('L1', 'L2') on a single or stitched C-arm image, but the labelling is an explicit manual act by the surgeon via a pull-down menu and drag-and-drop — there is no disclosure of automatic determination of which vertebra is which, and no claim recites labelling, naming or identifying a vertebra at all. The disclosure is therefore prior art to the *display* of level labels on a stitched fluoroscopic image, but not to automatic, algorithmic level identification or to abstention/region output.
confirmed.quote: The surgeon may also locate labels 250 identifying anatomic structure, in this case spinal vertebrae. ... For instance, activating the label button may access a pull down menu with the labels L 1, L 2, etc., and a drag and drop feature that allows the surgeon to place the labels at a desire location on the image.

confirmed.claim: The sole independent claim of US 12,223,118 B2 (claim 1; claims 2-16 all depend from it) requires the stored image to be derived from a three-dimensional representation of the surgical field, so like US 11,284,846 and US 10,368,956 it does not read, under the all-elements rule, on a method that uses only 2-D intraoperative radiographs and no preoperative volume.
confirmed.quote: A system for generating a display of an image of a patient's internal anatomy... a processor, in electronic communication with the memory and display, configured to: produce an image set that includes permutations of a first image, the first image being based on a three-dimensional representation of the surgical field including the patient's internal anatomy and being with respect to a baseline orientation, acquire a new image of the surgical field, select a representative image from the image set based on a correlation between the representative image and the new image, merge the selected representative image with the new image, and display the merged image on the display

confirmed.claim: Reciting concrete image-acquisition hardware and a closed-loop acquisition protocol did NOT rescue the claims at Alice step one. The '248 claim 1 required that a cellphone is used to acquire the analysis image; the '409 claim 1 required activation of an image acquisition apparatus, comparison of an image-quality attribute to a setpoint, and sending a message to guide the operator to retake the image, with claim 12 requiring the message be sent by the acquisition apparatus itself. All were held abstract and invalid. This directly qualifies the research question's premise that tying claims to a concrete imaging apparatus or acquisition protocol survives Alice — it is necessary but demonstrably not sufficient. A registration-free vertebra-naming claim reciting acquire overlapping C-arm exposures, analyze with a model, output a level name maps onto exactly the pattern the court rejected.
confirmed.quote: Claim 12 of the '409 patent is directed to the abstract idea of image acquisition, analysis via a deep learning device, comparison to a setpoint, and transmittal of the analysis result. ... Both claims thus fall within the familiar class of [patent-ineligible] claims that focus on collecting information, analyzing it, and displaying certain results of the collection and analysis.

confirmed.claim: Training a model on a large, specifically-curated, field-specific dataset confers no eligibility, because dataset specificity is treated as inherent to machine learning rather than as a technological improvement. The claims at issue expressly required a learning base comprising more than 1000 images of dental arches with per-tooth attribute labels, and the court held that limitation insufficient, citing Recentive Analytics, Inc. v. Fox Corp., 134 F.4th 1205, 1212 (Fed. Cir. 2025) (precedential; cert. denied, 146 S. Ct. 891 (2025)). This bears directly on the proposed invention's sequence model over per-vertebra embeddings trained on mixed band lengths — claiming the training-data regime (mixed band lengths, transitional-anatomy curation) will not by itself carry eligibility.
confirmed.quote: That a deep learning device be trained on a specific subset of data is incident to the very nature of machine learning, and thus is not a technological improvement rendering the claims eligible under § 101. See Recentive, 134 F.4th at 1212.

confirmed.claim: The technical advance must appear in the claim language itself; the court refused to credit an advance argued from the specification or from attorney characterization. Dental Monitoring argued its method was an advance in orthodontic technology itself enabling a more precise and objective assessment than previously possible, and the court rejected that because the claim did not recite the quantitative specificity asserted. The operative drafting rule for a registration-free level-ID claim is that the substituting-for-registration mechanism (the overlap linkage, the abstention/conformal rule, the disc-based delimitation rule) must be recited as claim limitations with concrete operative content, not described only in the specification.
confirmed.quote: Fatal to Dental Monitoring's argument is that it ignores the language of the claim itself; nothing in claim 14 requires a specific quantitative assessment beyond the ability of an orthodontist.

confirmed.claim: A specification that describes the model as selectable from off-the-shelf named networks is self-defeating at Alice step two, and eliminates the factual dispute that would otherwise defeat summary judgment under Berkheimer. The court held there was no genuine issue of material fact on conventionality precisely because the patents' own text listed commercially available neural networks (from e.g. Google or Microsoft). This is an actionable drafting constraint: do not write the model is preferably a neural network, e.g., ResNet/U-Net/a transformer if the model architecture is meant to supply the inventive concept.
confirmed.quote: There is no factual dispute regarding the generic nature of the deep learning device, because, as we note above, the patents themselves confirm its conventional nature. See '248 pat., col. 16 ll. 5-36 (confirming that the deep learning device could be chosen from neural networks made by, e.g., Google or Microsoft)

confirmed.claim: The guidance expressly adopts Stanford I/II as controlling on AI claims whose asserted advance is prediction accuracy: improving the accuracy of a mathematically calculated statistical prediction is an improvement to the abstract idea, not to technology, and therefore does not integrate the exception into a practical application at Step 2A Prong Two. This is the single largest 101 hazard for a vertebra-naming claim whose stated advance is higher naming accuracy (e.g. 97-99% at n vertebrae), and it argues for claiming the acquisition chain (overlapping C-arm exposures linked into a patient-specific chain) as the technological improvement rather than the accuracy number.
confirmed.quote: An improvement in the judicial exception itself is not an improvement in the technology. For example, in In re Board of Trustees of Leland Stanford Junior University, 989 F.3d 1367, 1370, 1373 (Fed. Cir. 2021) (Stanford I), the applicant claimed methods of resolving a haplotype phase involving steps of determining an inheritance state based on received allele data using a Hidden Markov Model. ... The applicant argued that the claimed process was an improvement over prior processes because it 'yields a greater number of haplotype phase predictions,' but the court found it was not 'an improved technological process' and instead was an improved 'mathematical process.' [fn 69: In re Board of Trs. of Leland Stanford Junior Univ., 991 F.3d 1245, 1251 (Fed. Cir. 2021) (Stanford II) (concluding that the claims are ineligible because the improvement in 'the accuracy of a mathematically calculated statistical prediction' is an improvement to the abstract idea (i.e., mathematical calculations) rather than an improvement to another technology).]

confirmed.claim: The operative Prong Two test the guidance states for AI inventions is whether the claim covers a particular solution to a problem or a particular way to achieve a desired outcome, versus merely the idea of the solution or outcome; the guidance names 'a specific application of AI to a particular technological field' as a qualifying form, citing Example 47 claim 3 (network intrusion detection) and Example 48 claims 2-3 (speech signal processing) as the templates. A registration-free level-ID claim should therefore be drafted as a specific application of AI to intraoperative fluoroscopic level confirmation with the particular mechanism recited, not as the outcome of naming a vertebra without a preoperative CT.
confirmed.quote: 'An important consideration in determining whether a claim improves technology is the extent to which the claim covers a particular solution to a problem or a particular way to achieve a desired outcome, as opposed to merely claiming the idea of a solution or outcome.' AI inventions may provide a particular way to achieve a desired outcome when they claim, for example, a specific application of AI to a particular technological field (i.e., a particular solution to a problem). [fn 68: Example 47, claim 3, claiming a specific application of AI to the field of network intrusion detection; and Example 48, claims 2 and 3, claiming a specific application of AI to the field of speech signal processing]

confirmed.claim: The opinion states the operative Alice step-one test as whether the claim focuses on a specific means or method that improves the relevant technology versus a result or effect — the doctrinal hinge for drafting an AI imaging claim around a named acquisition and processing mechanism (e.g. linking overlapping C-arm exposures into a chain) rather than around the output 'the vertebra is L4'.
confirmed.quote: we look to whether the claims 'focus on a specific means or method that improves the relevant technology or are instead directed to a result or effect that itself is the abstract idea and merely invoke generic processes and machinery.'

confirmed.claim: Under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) the disqualifying test is public availability itself, not the mechanism of disclosure: a disclosure that is neither a printed publication nor a sale is still prior art if the claimed invention was made sufficiently available to the public. For the inventor this means the disclosure clock can be started by artifacts that do not look like publications (a released weights file, a live demo, an open repo), and conversely that a genuinely access-controlled deployment is arguably outside the provision because nothing was made available to the public — though this MPEP section states the public-availability test without addressing password-gated or private-by-link access, so that boundary is not resolved here.
confirmed.quote: Even if a document or other disclosure is not a printed publication, or a transaction is not a sale, either may be prior art under the otherwise available to the public provision of AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1), provided that the claimed invention is made sufficiently available to the public.

refuted.claim: Every independent claim of US 10,368,956 B2 (method claim 1, system claim 11) requires as a mandatory first element receiving a preoperative 3D magnetic resonance image of the subject, so under the all-elements rule a method that never acquires any preoperative 3D volume cannot literally infringe any claim of this patent.

The limitation that keeps a registration-free vertebra-naming method outside every independent claim of US 8,718,346 is the permutation-set-and-merge machinery: each of claims 1, 33, 36 and 47 requires generating a 'baseline image set' of representative images at 'permutations of movements', then correlating a new lower-resolution image against that set and merging/displaying the selected representative image. A method that names vertebrae from overlapping C-arm exposures without building a permutation set of a prior baseline and without merging a stored baseline into the live image omits these elements, so it does not infringe under the all-elements rule.

The granted claims of US 12,223,118 are directed to image-quality restoration (merging a stored representative image with a live image to fill in anatomy obscured by instruments), not to naming or labelling vertebrae; vertebral labelling appears only in the specification, which makes this family prior-art-only disclosure on level identification rather than a blocking claim.

The specification of this family discloses stitching multiple separately acquired C-arm/fluoroscopic images into a composite panoramic base image, with an earliest priority of 6 October 2010 (Prov. 61/390,488) - an enabling public disclosure that predates and reads on element (a) of the proposed technique (linking a short series of overlapping C-arm exposures), even though it is not recited in any granted claim of this patent.

The guidance carves AI limitations out of the 'mental processes' abstract-idea grouping where the limitations cannot practically be performed in the human mind. This cuts directly at a vertebra-labelling claim: 'identify which vertebra this is' is exactly the observation/evaluation/judgment a radiologist performs mentally (counting down from C2), so a claim must be drafted around limitations the mind cannot practically perform (per-vertebra embeddings, a sequence model over mixed band lengths, a conformal abstention threshold) rather than around the identification result.

The Federal Circuit held that claims to a cardiac monitoring device that automates a diagnostic determination clinicians previously made by inspection are patent-eligible at Alice step one, reversing a Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal — establishing that a computer-implemented medical-diagnosis method is not abstract per se when framed as an improvement to the monitoring technology itself. (Retrieval note: the assigned Justia URL returned HTTP 403 to both WebFetch and curl; text was verified from caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-federal-circuit/2060703.html, the same opinion, U.S. Patent No. 7,941,207, decided April 17, 2020, before Dyk, Plager, and Stoll.)

The court grounded eligibility in concrete accuracy improvements recited in the written description — greater detection accuracy, high positive predictivity and sensitivity, avoidance of false positives and false negatives — meaning a specification that states measured performance gains (including an abstention/coverage tradeoff) is load-bearing for step one, not merely background.

unverified.claim: The surviving claim was an apparatus claim reciting named functional components (detectors, determination 'logic', an event generator) rather than a method of computing a diagnostic value — evidence that tying an algorithmic advance to recited device elements is a claim form that survives 101 at the Federal Circuit, notably without the components being novel hardware.
